title: Resourcing — Recruitment, Selection and Assessment Process Flow
subtitle: EEA 55 of 1998 (as amended 2022) · EE Regulations & Sectoral Targets 2025 · LRA · BCEA · ESA s.8 · Immigration Act 13 of 2002 · AARTO Act 46 of 1998 · POPIA · As at 19 October 2026

overview.summary: This flow tells an organisation what to do, by when, and who hands off to whom, from the moment a line manager raises a vacancy until the appointee has passed probation, the recruitment file is archived and the results feed back into the EE plan. It covers internal and external recruitment, promotions and succession appointments, and four ways of engaging the person chosen: permanent employment, a fixed-term contract, a TES placement, or the employment of a foreign national.

notes.text: Version 2.0 supersedes the GBS Resourcing — Organisational Recruitment and Selection Process Flow (v1, 30 September 2026). It keeps the v1 spine (Phases 0–6, the three designation paths, the three EE application models, forms RS01–RS42 and the verification register) and adds four variable gates. Each gate is answered and signed at step 1.11, before anything is published, and each opens a dedicated module with its own steps, forms and watch-points:
points: Gate A — Foreign nationals (Module A, section 10): could the appointee be a person who is not a South African citizen or permanent resident?
Gate B — EE plan targets and deviations (Module B, section 11): is an EE target at stake at this occupational level, and might the outcome depart from it?
Gate C — Driving roles and AARTO (Module C, section 12): will the appointee drive or control a vehicle for the employer?
Gate D — AI in recruitment (Module D, section 13): will any AI or automated tool source, screen, rank, interview, assess or communicate with candidates, or draft the advert?

notes.text: The flow runs one spine for every vacancy and splits where the law splits: at the designation decision (open, preferential or succession-linked post), at the variable gates, and at the engagement type. It assumes no collective agreement or bargaining council agreement regulates recruitment or promotion; where one does, it prevails and this flow must be adjusted. Public-service employers must also apply the Public Service Act and Regulations, which are not covered here.

notes.heading: Who uses it
notes.text: HR and talent acquisition (the process owner), line managers, EE managers, selection panels, delegated authorities, fleet managers (Module C), IT and AI system owners and the Information Officer (Module D), and legal or immigration advisers (Module A), in South African private-sector employers.

notes.heading: Legal status — employment equity
notes.text: The Employment Equity Amendment Act 4 of 2022 has been in force since 1 January 2025. Designated employers are employers with 50 or more employees, organs of state, municipalities and employers designated by a collective agreement. The Employment Equity Regulations, 2025 (GN 6125, GG 52515) and the Determination of Sectoral Numerical Targets (GN 6124, GG 52514) were published on 15 April 2025; the 2025 Regulations repealed the EE Regulations, 2014. The targets cover 18 sectors, the four upper occupational levels and a 3% target for persons with disabilities. EE plans for 1 September 2025 to 31 August 2030 must align with them (s.20(2A)). The NEASA and Sakeliga urgent application to suspend the targets (Part A) was dismissed by the High Court on 28 August 2025; leave to appeal was refused by the High Court (16 October 2025), the SCA (13 March 2026) and the Constitutional Court (reported 31 May–1 June 2026). Their non-urgent constitutional review (Part B), the BUSA review of the targets (filed September 2025) and the DA challenge are pending. A search on 19 October 2026 found no order suspending or setting aside the targets; the Department continues to implement them. The 2026 reporting cycle (online: 1 September 2026 to 15 January 2027) is the first in which progress against annual targets is assessed.

notes.heading: Legal status — foreign nationals
notes.text: The Immigration Act 13 of 2002 (s.38: no employment of an illegal foreigner or of a foreigner outside the terms of their status; s.49(3): offences), the Immigration Regulations, 2014 as amended (points-based assessment for general work and critical skills visas since 9 October 2024), the Critical Skills List (GN R3934, GG 49402, 3 October 2023, still operative; no new list was published in 2026), the Refugees Act 130 of 1998 as amended (s.22: asylum seekers may work only if the right is endorsed; employer letter within 14 days) and Employment Services Act 4 of 2014 s.8 are in force. The Employment Services Amendment Bill [B16-2026] is DRAFT ONLY: it is before Parliament and public comment closes on 6 November 2026. Module A includes a readiness note; a standalone GBS Foreign National Compliance flow is planned for when the Bill is final.

notes.heading: Legal status — AARTO
notes.text: Proclamations 322 and 323 of 2026 (GG 54917 and 54918, 29 June 2026) brought the operative AARTO provisions and most of the Amendment Act into force on 1 July 2026 in 62 municipalities (the 60 in Annexure A plus Johannesburg and Tshwane), with the AARTO Regulations, 2026. Phase 3 (about 151 further municipalities) has not been proclaimed: no Phase 3 proclamation had been gazetted as at 19 October 2026. On 4 August 2026 the RTIA told Parliament it expects Phase 3 in March 2027 (an earlier RTIA annual performance plan had pointed to October–December 2026). Until a proclamation is gazetted, only the 62 municipalities in Annexure A to Proclamation 323 of 2026 follow AARTO, and the AARTO duties in this flow (including s.17(5)) are law only there; elsewhere the Criminal Procedure Act regime continues and the same driver controls are best practice (GBS AARTO flow v1.1). Re-check at each 6.8 review. The demerit system (ss.24–28) and rehabilitation have not commenced; they are expected in a later phase with no date set.

notes.heading: Legal status — AI
notes.text: South Africa has no AI statute. The draft National AI Policy published for comment on 10 April 2026 was withdrawn on 26 April 2026 after fictitious citations were found (DLA Piper, 4 May 2026). POPIA s.71 (no decision based solely on automated processing) applies to AI screening, and the EEA s.8 duties apply to AI assessments that work like psychological tests. The Information Regulator has issued no s.71 or AI guidance as at 19 October 2026 (search).

notes.heading: Figures in force today
notes.text: BCEA earnings threshold: R269 600.90 a year from 1 May 2026 (previously R261 748.45). It decides who is protected by LRA ss.198A–198B and who may take an EEA s.10 dispute to CCMA arbitration. National minimum wage: R30.23 an hour from 1 March 2026 (separate EPWP and learnership rates apply; verify the current figures before use). Points-based visa income bands as published in October 2024: 50 points above R976 194 a year, 20 points from R650 976 to R976 194 (GN 5448 of 2024; verify any later adjustment).

notes.heading: Labels used throughout
points: LAW = a statute or regulation in force (EEA, LRA, BCEA, ESA, Immigration Act and Regulations, Refugees Act, AARTO Act and Regulations in proclaimed areas, NRTA, POPIA, PAIA, NCA and its Regulations, NQF Act, Children's Act, Criminal Law (Sexual Offences) Amendment Act, Health Professions Act). Binding now.

Code = a code of good practice: the Code on the Integration of EE into HR Policies and Practices (2005), the Code on the Employment of Persons with Disabilities (GN 1085, 9 November 2015) and the Code of Good Practice: Dismissal, 2025 (GN 3470, GG 53294, in force 4 September 2025; Schedule 8 repealed). Must be taken into account; departures must be justified.
CL = a principle from case law, cited by name, court and year. Verify the citation and any later authority before using it in advice. Non-reportable judgments are marked.

DRAFT = a Bill or draft instrument not in force: the Employment Services Amendment Bill [B16-2026], the Draft Reviewed Code of Good Practice on the EE Plan (GN 7719, GG 55046), the Revised White Paper proposals on immigration, and the AARTO demerit provisions (enacted but not commenced). Build readiness; do not treat as a current legal duty.

BP = best practice or internal control; not a statutory deadline. Adopt it as policy so it becomes binding internally. All weights, thresholds and periods marked BP are recommendations to be calibrated to each client.

notes.heading: Design principle
notes.text: In a recruitment dispute the employer carries the burden. Once an applicant alleges discrimination on a listed ground, the employer must prove that the conduct did not take place, was rational and not unfair, or was otherwise justifiable (EEA s.11). The 2025–2026 case law shows that employers lose mainly because EE considerations were brought in late, applied rigidly, or an approver overrode a panel without contemporaneous reasons. Version 2.0 applies the same rule to the four variables: every decision about right to work, EE targets and deviations, driving checks and AI tools is taken, recorded and signed before the vacancy goes to market (step 1.11, form RS60), and every later step leaves a record made at the time. That record is also the evidence for the Regulation 16(5) grounds, for a s.53 compliance certificate, for the Immigration Act s.38(2) good-faith defence and for POPIA accountability.

notes.heading: Fourteen interpretation points that shape the flow
points: Applicants are protected, but only by part of the law. For EEA ss.6, 7 and 8, "employee" includes an applicant for employment (s.9). LRA s.5(2) protects persons seeking employment against interference with union and LRA rights. An external applicant is not an "employee" for the unfair labour practice in LRA s.186(2)(a); only existing employees can claim an unfair promotion. External candidates therefore sue under the EEA, where the employer carries the onus.

Affirmative action is a defence, not a licence. Measures consistent with the EEA's purpose are not unfair discrimination (s.6(2)(a)), but they must flow from a current, consulted EE plan and be applied rationally and fairly (Constitution s.9(2); CL: Minister of Finance v Van Heerden, CC 2004; SAPS v Solidarity obo Barnard, CC 2014; Solidarity v Department of Correctional Services, CC 2016). A lapsed or unconsulted plan removes the defence.

No quotas and no absolute barriers. Affirmative action measures include preferential treatment and numerical goals but exclude quotas (s.15(3)); a designated employer need not create an absolute barrier to people outside the designated groups (s.15(4)). Non-designated applicants must still be able to be considered. A rational pipeline tied to EE targets is a lawful restitutionary measure, and shortlisting within it is not an absolute barrier where others can still be motivated and considered (CL: Eskom Holdings v Solidarity obo Erasmus [2025] ZALAC 55, LAC, 5 November 2025, overturning the Labour Court).

"Suitably qualified" is broad. Formal qualifications, prior learning, relevant experience, or the capacity to acquire the ability to do the job within a reasonable time, considered together; no unfair discrimination solely on lack of relevant experience (s.20(3)–(5)). Every person specification must state equivalents, not only minimums.

Timing decides lawfulness. Preference introduced after interviews, with no plan behind it, is unfair discrimination (CL: Moses Kotane Institute v Mzimele, LAC 2026). Using targets as the sole reason to reject the panel's top candidate, where no suitable under-represented candidate was realistically available, is irrational and unfair (CL: Solidarity obo Benjamin v Department of Correctional Services, LC, June 2026, non-reportable: 12 months' compensation). The designation, the EE model and the deviation route are therefore fixed in Phase 1.

The correct target set. Annual targets must align with the s.15A targets for the employer's sector (the sector in which most employees are engaged, Reg 9(7)(c)), and the Impact Note must use the target set the plan actually uses: national, regional or plan-specific. Benjamin turned partly on national figures being applied where the plan also set regional targets. Where a group already exceeds the EAP, avoid perpetuating the over-representation (Reg 9(10)).

Deviations are lawful if structured in advance. Targets are not quotas; a designated employer may appoint outside the target direction where no suitably qualified target-group candidate is appointable, provided the deviation is motivated, approved at the pre-set level, recorded and reported (Reg 16(5); Module B). An unrecorded deviation is evidence against the employer in an EE assessment; an unjustified refusal to deviate is evidence against it in a Benjamin-type claim.

Promotions: a fair process, not a right. No right to be promoted, but a right to a fair and rational process that follows the employer's own policy (LRA s.186(2)(a); CL: Noonan v SSSBC, LAC 2012; Head of Department of Education v Mofokeng, LAC 2014). Acting in a post confers no right to it (CL: Hlope v HOD: Education KZN, LC 2024, verify).

Acceptance can create employment. A person who has accepted an offer but not started may already be an "employee"; withdrawing the offer can be a dismissal (CL: Wyeth SA v Manqele, LAC 2005). Offers are therefore always expressly conditional, including on a valid visa (Module A) and a valid licence and PrDP for driving roles (Module C).

Testing is regulated twice. Medical testing is prohibited unless legislation permits or requires it or it is justifiable (s.7(1)); HIV testing needs a Labour Court order (s.7(2)). Psychological and similar assessments must be scientifically shown to be valid and reliable, capable of fair application to all employees, and not biased (s.8(a)–(c)). The HPCSA certification requirement (former s.8(d)), which Association of Test Publishers v President of the RSA (GNP 2017) found unworkable, was deleted by the Employment Equity Amendment Act 4 of 2022 with effect from 1 January 2025; the employer bears the onus on (a)–(c), and HPCSA classification and practitioner rules still apply to psychological tests.

A human decides. A candidate may not be subjected to a decision with legal consequences, or which affects them to a substantial degree, based solely on automated processing that profiles them, unless a s.71(2) exception applies with appropriate measures: an opportunity to make representations and enough information about the logic to make them meaningful (POPIA s.71(3)). AI video, game and chatbot scoring of personality or ability is also a "similar assessment" under EEA s.8 (Module D).

Right to work is a gate, not a preference. No employer may employ a foreign national before the person produces a valid visa or permit authorising that work (ESA s.8(1); Immigration Act s.38(1)), and the employer must make a good-faith effort to check (s.38(2)). Citizenship is part of the designated-group test: only black people, women and people with disabilities who are South African citizens by birth or descent, or who were naturalised before 27 April 1994 (or later, if apartheid policies prevented earlier naturalisation), are "designated groups" (EEA s.1). Foreign nationals, permanent residents and other post-1994 naturalised citizens do not count towards EE targets, so appointing one to a preferential post is a deviation (Module B). Excluding permanent residents is high-risk (CL: Larbi-Odam v MEC for Education (North-West Province), CC 1997).

Driving checks follow the job, not the person. Licence, PrDP and AARTO checks are justified only where driving or controlling a vehicle is an inherent requirement identified at job analysis, and only at final-candidate stage with notice and consent. Demerit points cannot be used because the system has not commenced; an outstanding AARTO enforcement order matters because it blocks the issue of a licence or PrDP until resolved (AARTO Act s.20(5)) (Module C).

Foreign workers without papers are still employees. A contract with a foreign national who lacks a valid visa is not void for LRA purposes; the worker may still claim (ESA s.8(4); CL: Discovery Health v CCMA, LC 2008). A lapsed visa is a reason to stop the work lawfully, not to ignore fair procedure.

notes.heading: Roles used
notes.text: Talent Acquisition / HR recruiter (TA, the process owner and spine); Line Manager (LM, the hiring manager); EE Manager (EEM, the senior manager assigned under s.24); EE / Consultative Forum (EEF); Selection Panel (PNL) and its Chair (CHR); Subject-matter Expert (SME); Talent Committee (TC); Delegated Authority (DA); Executive Committee or CEO (EXCO); Legal / IR (LA); Immigration adviser or registered practitioner (IMM); Information Officer (IO, POPIA); AI System Owner (AIO, the business owner of each AI tool); IT / ATS owner (IT); Fleet Manager (FM); AARTO Compliance Officer (ACO, from the GBS AARTO flow); registered Psychologist or Psychometrist (PSY); Occupational Health Practitioner (OHP); Payroll and Finance (PAY, FIN); Board (BOARD). Candidates (CAND), including internal candidates (INT), the succession candidate (SUC) and foreign-national candidates (FNC); union observer where a collective agreement provides (UO). External: private employment agency (AGY); temporary employment service (TES); verification vendor (VV); AI vendor (AIV); SAQA and the NLRD; SAPS Criminal Record Centre; credit bureaus; professional bodies; Department of Home Affairs (DHA); Department of Employment and Labour and ESSA (DEL); Road Traffic Infringement Agency (RTIA) and eNaTIS; driving licence testing centres (DLTC); CCMA; Labour Court (LC); Information Regulator (IR).

stages.title: Phase 0 — Readiness (standing obligations)
intro: Phase 0 has no case trigger. It must be in place before the first vacancy is raised, because the lawfulness of preference, the validity of every assessment and AI tool, the POPIA basis for every check, the right-to-work procedure and the driver-check rules are all decided by documents that must already exist. Steps 0.16–0.19 are new in v2.0 and set up the four modules.

notes.heading: Candidate side of Phase 0
notes.text: Nothing is owed yet, but candidates' later rights depend on this phase. A candidate screened out by a tool that was never validated, by a credit check for a role that was never certified, or by a driver check for a role that does not drive has a strong claim whatever the merits.

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: An EE plan that has expired or was never consulted leaves every preferential decision without a defence (CL: Solidarity obo Pretorius v City of Tshwane, LC 2016: expired plan, no defence). Check the plan dates, the AI register and the driving-role list before the first requisition of every year.

stages.title: Phase 1 — Vacancy, job analysis, designation and variable gates
intro: Day 0 is the day the line manager raises the requisition. Phase 1 must be finished before anything is published, because the advert must state the requirements, the equivalents, the EE position and the notices the gates require, and none of these may change afterwards (CL: Moses Kotane, LAC 2026). Phase 1 produces five governing documents: the Vacancy EE Impact Note, the person specification, the competency profile, the Designation Decision Record, and the Variable Gates Record (RS60).

notes.heading: Candidate obligations at this stage
notes.text: None; candidates are not yet involved. An internal or foreign-national candidate proposed by the line manager must be declared at step 1.1.

notes.heading: Hand-offs
notes.text: LM → TA (requisition). TA → EEM (Impact Note, pool analysis). TA → TC (succession check). EEM → DA (designation). TA → FM (driving role), AIO (tools), LA or IMM (foreign national) for Gate answers. LA → DA (review). TA → FIN (band).

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: Designating a post "preferential" after candidates are known, earmarking a post contrary to the plan, or adding a driver check or an AI screening tool after the advert, are all late changes that the record will expose. The Designation Decision Record and RS60 must bear dates earlier than the advert.

stages.title: Phase 2 — Sourcing, advertising and applications
intro: The advert fixes what the employer may later rely on. Criteria added afterwards, or a material departure from it, require re-advertising (CL: Moses Kotane). Phase 2 also fixes the POPIA basis for everything later done with candidate information, including driver records and AI processing, and starts the local-search record that Module A needs.

notes.heading: Candidate obligations at this stage
notes.text: Submit a complete application by the closing date; give truthful information about qualifications, registrations, right-to-work status, licences and history (a false qualification claim is an offence, NQF Act s.32B); disclose any need for accommodation; follow the AI-use statement.

notes.heading: Hand-offs
notes.text: TA → AGY (brief). TA → channels (publication). TA → IO (privacy notice). TA → LA or IMM (local-search record). CAND → TA (applications, EEA1, accommodation requests).

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: The privacy notice must name the verification vendors, any AI vendor and any automated tool. A check run by a vendor the candidate was never told about, or a ranking by a tool that was not disclosed, is unlawful processing even if the check itself was justified.
Open post.

[Employer] is an equal opportunity employer committed to employment equity under its Employment Equity Plan. All suitably qualified applicants are encouraged to apply. Persons with disabilities are invited to apply and to indicate any reasonable accommodation required during the selection process. Appointment is subject to the right to work in South Africa.
Preferential post.

This position forms part of [Employer]'s Employment Equity Plan for [occupational level]. In line with that Plan and the applicable sectoral targets, preference will be given to suitably qualified candidates from the following designated groups: [e.g. African women; persons with disabilities]. All suitably qualified applicants are welcome to apply and will be considered. "Suitably qualified" includes formal qualifications, recognised prior learning, relevant experience, or the capacity to acquire the ability to do the job within a reasonable time. [Employer] reserves the right not to make an appointment.
Succession-linked post (internal ring-fenced phase).

Internal advertisement. This role is being filled through [Employer]'s Talent and Succession Programme. Applications are invited from all permanent employees at [grade/level] who meet the requirements below. Candidates identified in the succession pool, and any other eligible employee, will be assessed through the same structured process. In line with our Employment Equity Plan, preference may be given to suitably qualified candidates from [designated groups]. If no suitable internal candidate is identified, the role will be advertised externally.
Driving role (add to any of the above).

Driving is an inherent requirement of this role. Applicants must hold a valid Code [C1/EC] driving licence [and a Professional Driving Permit, category [G/P/D]]. Final candidates will be asked to consent to verification of their licence and PrDP and to disclose any outstanding AARTO enforcement order or licence suspension. Traffic fines alone will not disqualify an applicant.
AI notice (where Gate D is open).

We use [tool] to [schedule interviews / answer questions / organise applications]. No application is rejected by a computer: a member of our recruitment team reviews every decision. You may ask for an explanation or a review by a person at [contact]. See our candidate privacy notice for details.

Direct appointment without advertising is defensible only where the recruitment policy or a collective agreement expressly allows it, the successor was identified through the documented talent process (step 0.6), and the EEM and DA sign off (CL: Mofokeng, LAC 2014).

stages.title: Phase 5 — Offer, contracting and onboarding
intro: Phase 5 turns an approved selection into a lawful engagement. The offer is always conditional; the medical assessment, where justified, comes after it; the contract follows the engagement type; and onboarding starts the probation clock. The four engagement tracks share steps 5.1–5.6. Track 5D is now driven by Module A; driver onboarding by Module C.

stages.group: Module D — Use of AI in recruitment
stages.title: Module D — Use of AI in recruitment
intro: For each tool, and at each stage it affects, compare selection rates by race, gender and disability (and age band where relevant). Flag a group whose rate is below four-fifths of the highest group's rate, and confirm with a significance test where numbers allow; with small numbers, pool over several vacancies. The four-fifths rule is a US screening heuristic, not SA law, but it gives a defensible, consistent trigger for the s.8 and s.11 onus. Record the test, the result and the action (RS56): continue, re-weight, re-configure, replace, or stop. Test before first use with vendor or pilot data, then at least annually and whenever the model or configuration changes.

Ask every vendor, in writing, before contract: what the tool decides or recommends; the features used and excluded; training data and whether it includes South African data; validity evidence for the stated purpose; adverse-impact results by SA designated groups; explainability for s.71(3) representations; human-override design; data hosting and cross-border transfers; sub-processors; security; retention and deletion; audit and logging; change notification; liability and indemnity. A vendor that cannot answer the validity and adverse-impact questions cannot be used for screening or assessment.

intro: Module A opens when Gate A is answered "yes" at step 1.11: the role is open to foreign applicants, a foreign-national candidate is known, or an agency or TES may supply one. It applies the law in force on 19 October 2026. It does not apply the Employment Services Amendment Bill [B16-2026], which is a DRAFT; the readiness note at the end of this section sets out what to prepare. A standalone GBS Foreign National Compliance flow is planned for when the Bill is final; until then, this module is the GBS procedure.
The legal frame in force.

Immigration Act 13 of 2002, s.38. No person may employ an illegal foreigner, a foreigner whose status does not authorise employment by that person, or a foreigner in a capacity not in accordance with their status (s.38(1)). An employer must make a good-faith effort to ascertain that it employs no illegal foreigner and to establish the status or citizenship of those it employs (s.38(2)). Knowledge is presumed once illegal employment is shown unless the employer proves good faith and compliance with s.38(2); stricter compliance is required of an employer with more than five employees or a previous conviction (s.38(3)). The employer must keep the prescribed records for two years after the employment ends and report to the Department the end of the employment and any breach of status (s.38(4)). A person in control of premises where an illegal foreigner is found employed is presumed to employ them (s.38(5)). Knowingly employing an illegal foreigner, or a foreigner in breach of the Act, is an offence: a fine or up to one year on a first conviction, up to two years or a fine on a second, and up to five years without the option of a fine on a third or later conviction (s.49(3)).

Immigration Regulations, 2014 as amended. Since 9 October 2024 (Third Amendment), general work and critical skills work visas are assessed on a 100-point system: occupation on the Critical Skills List (100 points); qualifications; experience; official-language proficiency; income bands; and an offer from an employer in the Trusted Employer Scheme (30 points; phase II window 20 July – 4 September 2026; verify the directive number, reported as Immigration Directive 10 of 2024). Secondary sources report that points-based applicants no longer need the DEL recommendation letter for a general work visa (verify on the DHA checklist). Record-keeping and termination reporting are statutory duties under s.38(4) of the Act (above).

Critical Skills List. GN R3934, GG 49402, 3 October 2023, remains the operative list; no new list was published in 2026. A critical-skills applicant needs a job offer from an employer that is verifiable and in good standing with DEL, and professional-body confirmation; since 8 October 2024 a visa can be issued for 12 months while a SAQA evaluation is pending.

Refugees Act 130 of 1998 as amended. An asylum seeker may work only if the right to work is endorsed on the asylum seeker visa after the s.22(6) assessment; it may not be endorsed for an applicant who can support themselves or is supported by UNHCR or a charity (s.22(8)). The employer must give the Department a letter of employment in the prescribed form (Form 6 of the Refugees Regulations) within 14 days of the person starting work (s.22(9)); failure, or a fraudulent letter, is an offence with a fine of up to R20 000 (s.22(10)). The endorsement is revoked if the holder cannot prove employment within 6 months (s.22(11)). A recognised refugee may seek employment (s.27(f)).

Employment Services Act 4 of 2014. An employer may not employ a foreign national before the person produces an applicable and valid work permit issued under the Immigration Act (s.8(1)), and may not require or permit a foreign national to do work the permit does not authorise or to work contrary to its terms (s.9(1)). An employee employed without a valid permit may still enforce any claim against the employer (s.8(4)). Section 8(2) allows the Minister to make regulations requiring employers to be satisfied that no suitably skilled person in South Africa is available, to use public or private employment services, and to prepare a skills-transfer plan; no final regulations imposing these duties were identified (verify). "Foreign national" excludes permanent residence permit holders (s.1).

Equal treatment and fair process. A foreign national is protected by the EEA and LRA like any other employee; nationality and citizenship discrimination must be justified (CL: Larbi-Odam, CC 1997, on permanent residents). A contract with a worker who lacks a valid permit is not void for LRA purposes (CL: Discovery Health v CCMA, LC 2008).

EE interplay. Foreign nationals, permanent residents and citizens naturalised after 26 April 1994 (unless apartheid policies prevented earlier naturalisation) are not members of the designated groups (EEA s.1). They are reported in the EEA2 as foreign nationals and do not advance any target. An appointment to a preferential post is a deviation (Module B).

intro: The Bill was introduced in the National Assembly in 2026 (prior notice of introduction in GG 54759, 29 May 2026) to implement the National Labour Migration Policy. The Portfolio Committee called for comment on 18 September 2026; public comment closes on 6 November 2026. It is not law and may change. As introduced it would: require an employer, before recruiting a foreign national, to be satisfied in a prescribed manner that no one other than a foreign national in South Africa has the necessary skills (proposed s.12A); require a skills-transfer plan for any position held by a foreign national, with ministerial exclusions; allow the Minister to set maximum foreign-national quotas by sector, occupation, region or nationally after a 30-day comment period, with small employers (generally fewer than 10 employees) excluded and exemptions under a new s.49A (proposed s.12B); require terms not inferior to those of South African citizens and retention of visa and right-to-work records (proposed s.12A(2)(d)–(e)); prohibit requiring or permitting work outside a visa's scope (proposed s.12E); allow inspectors and bargaining council agents to enforce claims (proposed s.12D); and set penalties, per employer and per contravention of proposed ss.12A, 12B(8) and 12E (proposed s.49(2A)), of R100 000 for a first contravention, R200 000 for a repeat within three years, and the greater of R1 million or 10% of turnover for further contraventions. The legal frame. Compliance is assessed by the Director-General, who must consider whether the employer has a reasonable justification for not meeting targets (s.42 as amended); the EE Regulations, 2025 list seven reasonable grounds (Reg 16(5)) and tie the s.53 compliance certificate to them (Reg 16(7)).

intro: Case law that shapes the deviation route.

Solidarity obo Benjamin v Department of Correctional Services (LC, June 2026, non-reportable). The panel's top candidate was refused because the appointment would not advance national targets. The court held the decision irrational and unfair: the decision-maker did not engage with the panel's recommendation, relied solely on numerical targets, used national figures where the plan also had regional targets, and did not consider whether a suitable under-represented candidate was realistically available before re-advertising. Targets should have been "a neutral factor" with merit decisive. Award: 12 months' compensation. Lesson: the pool analysis and the deviation route must exist before the decision, and the approver must engage with the panel in writing.

Moses Kotane Institute v Mzimele (LAC 2026). A gender requirement introduced after interviews, by an employer with no EE plan, was unfair discrimination and an absolute barrier to male candidates. Press reports refer to a damages award of about R4.52 million; verify the LAC's final order on damages before citing it. Lesson: the model cannot be changed after the advert.

Eskom Holdings v Solidarity obo Erasmus [2025] ZALAC 55 (LAC, 5 November 2025). The LAC overturned a Labour Court finding of race discrimination: a known pipeline practice tied to EE targets was a rational restitutionary measure, and it was not an absolute barrier because non-designated candidates could still be motivated, shortlisted and interviewed. Lesson: preference is defensible when it is target-linked, documented and leaves others able to compete; write the pipeline into the plan or policy so it can be proved.
Barnard (CC 2014), Solidarity v DCS (CC 2016), Van Heerden (CC 2004). Measures must be rational, plan-based and not rigid quotas.

intro: Module C opens when Gate C is answered "yes": the appointee will drive or control a vehicle for the employer (company, pool, hired or own vehicle on business). It decides whether driving is inherent, what may be checked and when, what may and may not be used to reject, and how the appointee is made ready to be nominated as a driver under AARTO before the first trip.
The legal frame.

AARTO rollout. In force since 1 July 2026 in 62 municipalities under Proclamations 322 and 323 of 2026 (GG 54917 and 54918, 29 June 2026) and the AARTO Regulations, 2026. Elsewhere the Criminal Procedure Act regime continues. Phase 3 (about 151 further municipalities) has not been proclaimed; no proclamation had been gazetted as at 19 October 2026. On 4 August 2026 the RTIA told Parliament it expects Phase 3 in March 2027 (an earlier RTIA annual performance plan had pointed to October–December 2026). Until a proclamation is gazetted, only the 62 municipalities in Annexure A to Proclamation 323 of 2026 follow AARTO. Map the role's routes against Annexure A (GBS AARTO flow step 0.8).

Demerit system not in force. Sections 24–28 (points, suspension, cancellation) and the rehabilitation programme were excluded from the proclamations and are expected in a later phase with no date set. No demerit points may be used in recruitment. Section 33 (employer checking a person's demerit status with written permission on AARTO 27) is of no practical use until points exist.

Owner and operator duties. An owner or operator who allows a person to drive or control a vehicle must first obtain the driver's full names, identity document, and residential, postal, business and email addresses (AARTO Act s.17(5)). These particulars make a nomination within 32 days possible (s.17(1)(f)(v), s.17(4)). The duty is law only in AARTO municipalities; apply it everywhere as policy so that drivers can be nominated wherever a notice is issued. Onboarding steps C.9–C.11 deliver them (GBS AARTO flow steps 0.5–0.7).

Enforcement orders. Until an enforcement order is complied with or revoked, no driving licence, PrDP, permit or licence disc may be issued to the person (AARTO Act s.20(5)). An outstanding order can therefore stop a driver renewing a licence or PrDP. Unpaid infringement notices and courtesy letters do not have that effect on their own. A PrDP is valid for 24 months (NRTR reg 122(1)).

National Road Traffic Act 93 of 1996. A driving licence of the correct code is required to drive; a Professional Driving Permit is required for specified vehicles and purposes (goods vehicles above prescribed masses, passenger-carrying and dangerous goods) and must be renewed every 24 months with medical fitness (NRTR reg 122(1)). Licence authenticity and validity are verified on eNaTIS, directly where the employer has access or through an accredited vendor or DLTC.

POPIA. Licence and PrDP data are personal information; criminal driving convictions are special personal information (s.26); AARTO infringements are administrative, but treat them with the same care. Lawful basis: steps linked to concluding the contract at the candidate's request (s.11(1)(b)) and legitimate interest (s.11(1)(f)) for licence and PrDP verification; written consent (RS52) for AARTO portal and conviction checks; legal obligation (s.11(1)(c)) for the s.17(5) particulars at onboarding. Notice under s.18 at collection.

Proportionality and equality. Driving requirements in a job that does not need them disadvantage groups less likely to hold licences and may be indirect discrimination (EEA s.6(1)); they are justified only as inherent requirements (s.6(2)(b)).

intro: Module D opens when Gate D is answered "yes": any AI or automated tool will source or contact candidates, draft the advert or job description, parse, screen, rank or match applications, run a chatbot, schedule, transcribe or summarise interviews, or score video, game-based or written assessments. It also covers candidates' own use of AI. It links to the GBS AI Compliance flow and the GBS POPIA flow, both being built in parallel, and to the GBS AI Policy.
The legal frame.

POPIA s.71. A data subject may not be subjected to a decision with legal consequences, or which affects them to a substantial degree, based solely on automated processing intended to profile them, including their performance at work. The exceptions in s.71(2) (a decision in connection with concluding or executing a contract, or one governed by a law or code that specifies appropriate measures) apply only in limited cases: a contract-related decision is exempt outright only where the data subject's request has been met (s.71(2)(a)(i)), which is never the case for a rejection; otherwise appropriate measures are needed: an opportunity to make representations and sufficient information about the underlying logic (s.71(3)). The safe design is that no tool takes a rejection decision: a human with authority reviews every adverse outcome.

Other POPIA conditions. Notice at collection (s.18), including AI use and cross-border flows; minimality and purpose (ss.10, 13); collection from the candidate unless an exception applies (s.12), which rules out scraping social profiles; retention (s.14); security (s.19); operator contracts with AI vendors (ss.20–21); special personal information such as race, health or biometrics from video analysis (ss.26–33); cross-border transfers to offshore hosts (s.72). Administrative fines up to R10 million (s.109).

EEA ss.6, 8 and 11. An AI tool that infers personality, ability or "fit" is a "similar assessment" that must be valid, reliable, fairly applied and unbiased (s.8); a tool that screens out a designated group disproportionately is indirect discrimination unless justified (s.6); the employer carries the onus (s.11) and cannot pass it to the vendor.

No AI statute or guidance. No binding AI law; the draft National AI Policy (10 April 2026) was withdrawn on 26 April 2026 (verify); no Information Regulator guidance on s.71 or AI as at 19 October 2026.

Cases: Hlope (LC 2024), Reynhardt v UNISA (LAC 2010), SAPU obo Singh v SAPS (secondary sources only); the LAC's order on damages in Moses Kotane.

No external validation route for EEA s.8. Since s.8(d) (HPCSA certification) was deleted with effect from 1 January 2025, no body certifies tests or AI assessments; employers alone carry the s.8(a)–(c) onus, so vendor evidence and local adverse-impact testing (RS55, RS56) are the only proof.
POPIA s.71 has no guidance. Nothing says when human involvement is enough to take a decision out of "solely" automated processing. The Module D safeguards are prudent, not settled.
Sectoral targets cover only the four upper levels. Preference at lower levels still needs plan-based numerical goals; the Regulations do not say how the two interact.
Regulation 16(5) evidence has no prescribed form and no deviation-approval standard. Module B supplies one; the final Code on the EE Plan (DRAFT GN 7719) may fill the gap.

B16-2026 and the EEA. Foreign-national quotas by sector and occupation would sit alongside EE sectoral targets, but the Bill does not say how the two are reconciled for the same vacancy, or whether a foreign national appointed under a quota is a reasonable ground under Reg 16(5).

AARTO and recruitment. The Act gives employers a demerit-check mechanism (s.33, AARTO 27) for a system not yet in force, and no mechanism for checking enforcement orders against a candidate except through consent and the portal.
NQF Act s.32A(1) is unproclaimed, and NCA reg 18(4)(c) does not define "a position that requires honesty in dealing with cash or finances".
Unfair labour practice gap for external candidates. LRA s.186(2)(a) protects only employees.
